evidence: The same bullet later says the topology is UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED and must be costed separately.

correction: Replace 'doubles' with 'can roughly double or more, depending on failover and replication policy; must be costed separately.'

quoted_clause: The benefit of many requests sharing the same retrieved-context prefix belongs to prefix caching — a distinct mechanism (Ch 2 §2.1, developed in Ch 11) — not to continuous batching.
observed: The prefix-caching / KV-reuse definition lives in Ch 2 §1 (Concept), in the 'A vocabulary note that prevents a common conflation' table. Ch 2 §2 is the Mental Model and has no subsections, so '§2.1' resolves to nothing. The book's own §-notation elsewhere is §chapter.section ('§4.3' = Ch 4 §3 Worked Example; '§3.6' = Ch 3 §6 Architecture Consequence), which makes '§2.1' malformed under either reading.
evidence: Ch 2 section headings: '## 1. Concept' (contains the vocabulary table), '## 2. Mental Model', '## 3. Worked Example'. No §2.1 exists.

correction: Change to '(Ch 2 §1, developed in Ch 11)'. While in the file, normalise the §-notation so that '§chapter.section' is used unambiguously everywhere — 'Ch 3 §3.6' (Ch 3 mini-case) currently reads as 'section 3.6' but means Ch 3 §6.
acceptance_test: Every '§n.m' pointer in the manuscript resolves to an existing section, and the notation is stated once in the front matter.

quoted_clause: Input-to-output ratio: 9,200 ÷ 300 ≈ 30× more input tokens than output tokens. This ratio is [canonical scenario][DERIVED] from the canonical numbers and is the single biggest factor in why this workload is KV-capacity- and prefill-dominated rather than decode-throughput-limited.
observed: The input/output ratio is a signal, not the single determinant. KV capacity depends on context length and concurrency; decode can dominate wall-clock latency even in input-heavy workloads. The chapter itself later says decode is ~87% of per-request wall-clock.
evidence: Ch 2 and Ch 4 both distinguish resource regime from wall-clock latency; measured per-phase utilization and goodput are required to confirm dominance.
root_cause: Claim strength exceeds the evidence.
correction: Soften to 'a first signal' and point to measured per-phase utilization and goodput before concluding dominance.
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer claims a single biggest factor; it cross-references Ch 2/Ch 8 and the need for measurement.

page_hint: Ch 4, §8 mini-case, second paragraph (compare Ch 1, §8 mini-case, second paragraph)
quoted_clause: From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone, the architect can already establish: the unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output; the workload is input-heavy; and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request, because every downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible) is priced against it.
observed: This is a near-verbatim restatement of Ch 1's mini-case closing paragraph ('From the token-level work alone ... the unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output; the working hypothesis is input-heavy ...; and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request, because every downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible) is priced against it.'). The repetition adds nothing: Ch 4's mini-case is supposed to deliver the six-dimension payoff, and instead opens by replaying Ch 1's payoff. This is class-C redundant repetition, not reinforcement.
evidence: Side-by-side comparison of the two paragraphs: identical clause sequence (unit is tokens / request shape / input-heavy / first number to lock down / downstream decisions priced against it), differing only in 'the working hypothesis is input-heavy (Ch 4 quantifies it)' → 'the workload is input-heavy'.
root_cause: The continuous-scenario mini-case template was applied to Ch 4 without replacing the inherited Ch 1 framing with the chapter's own deliverable.
correction: Delete the replayed paragraph and open Ch 4's mini-case on the six-dimension projection itself: the stakeholder's ask ('thousands of employees, accurate and fast') mapped onto the six axes, with the two axes that are *not* yet quantified (quality threshold, economic ceiling) named as the missing inputs, then the growth variant (5,000 employees, 50 rps) sized. Keep one sentence of continuity ('the unit is tokens, established in Ch 1') rather than a paragraph.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 4's mini-case appears in Ch 1's mini-case; the mini-case's first paragraph contains at least one quantity or distinction that exists only in Ch 4.

quoted_clause: a 70B FP16 model on one host meets the per-request latency SLO (TTFT/TPOT)
observed: Ch 2's arithmetic is a first-order analytical lower bound that excludes attention overhead, MFU, communication, and scheduling. 'Meets' overstates what has been shown.
evidence: Ch 2 repeatedly labels the arithmetic 'Analytical bound — not a benchmark'; Ch 4 later says both bounds must be confirmed by benchmark goodput.
root_cause: Claim strength exceeds the analytical evidence.
correction: Say 'is analytically feasible under the first-order model; benchmark confirmation is required.'
acceptance_test: The sentence carries the analytical/benchmark qualifier.

page_hint: Ch 4, §3 sidebar table 'what the ~$15,000 budget line is, and the 6–21-host workload comparison', 'Per 1K req' column and its footnote
quoted_clause: The *Per 1K req* column divides *Monthly* by the canonical request volume: **~6.24M active-hours requests/month** (10 rps × 3,600 s × 8 h × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 ...)
observed: The 'Per 1K req' column divides a *peak-capacity* numerator (the 21-host always-on-at-peak row, $306,600) by an *average-volume* denominator (6.24M requests/month at the 10 rps average). The resulting ~$49.13/1K req is neither the cost of serving average traffic nor the cost of serving peak traffic; it is the cost of peak capacity amortized over average volume. The row labels ('always-on at peak', 'peak KV-screen fleet') do not carry that meaning, and the column header invites the reader to read it as a per-request cost at the stated traffic. The same mixing appears in the mini-case ('$306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K').
evidence: 6.24M requests/month is the 10 rps average volume (10 × 3600 × 8 × 260 ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 ✓). The 21-host row's monthly figure is peak-provisioned capacity ($306,600). At the 40 rps peak the monthly volume would be 24.96M, giving $306,600 ÷ 24,960K ≈ $12.28/1K req — half the printed number.
root_cause: A single 'Per 1K req' column was applied to rows whose numerators are priced at different operating points, without normalizing the denominator to match.
correction: Split the column into 'per 1K req @ average volume' and 'per 1K req @ peak volume', or add an explicit 'volume basis' column stating which request volume each row's numerator is paired with. If the intent is 'cost of peak capacity amortized over average volume', rename the column accordingly (e.g. 'peak-capacity cost per 1K avg-volume req').
acceptance_test: Every row in the sidebar table states the request volume its per-1K-req figure is divided by, and the peak row's figure is not readable as a per-request cost at the average traffic.

quoted_clause: At 10 concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB of KV on top of the 140 GB weights — pressing against the 640 GB pool well before concurrency reaches 100.
observed: At 10 concurrent requests, 241 GB KV + 140 GB weights = 381 GB, leaving ~259 GB free. The pool is not 'pressing' at 10; it becomes tight around ~20 full-context requests.
root_cause: Imprecise wording.
correction: State the actual total at 10 requests and the approximate concurrency at which the pool tightens.
acceptance_test: The sentence gives 381 GB at 10 requests and says the pool tightens around ~20, not at 10.

page_hint: Ch 4, §3 'Cost-basis distinction (do not confuse the two)' table, second row, Derivation cell
quoted_clause: ($120/hr whole-fleet at ~6 hosts) / (92K inp tok/s + 3K out tok/s) converted to per-million-tokens via 3600 | ~$0.362 / 1M input tokens (i.e. ~2.76M input tokens per cloud dollar), ~$11.11 / 1M output tokens (~90K output per cloud dollar).
observed: The derivation shown (dividing by the combined 95K tok/s) produces the blended rate $0.3509/1M combined, not the two split rates printed in the same cell ($0.362/1M input and $11.11/1M output). The cell's own prose later gives the blended figure, so the derivation cell and the numbers cell describe different operations. A reader following the printed derivation will not reproduce the printed numbers.
root_cause: The cell was edited to add the blended rate and the split rates without updating the derivation string.
correction: Rewrite the derivation cell to show the two separate divisions explicitly ('$120/hr ÷ 92,000 tok/s → $0.362/1M input; $120/hr ÷ 3,000 tok/s → $11.11/1M output; blended over 95,000 tok/s → $0.3509/1M combined') and move the combined rate into the same cell as a third, clearly-labelled figure.
acceptance_test: The derivation cell's arithmetic, followed literally, yields each of the three numbers printed in the cell.

quoted_clause: long enough for Little's Law and service-time occupancy to reach the modeled steady state (seconds of sustained 40 rps)
observed: Little's Law steady state requires at least the service-time scale W ≈ 8.6 s, not merely 'seconds.' A 2-second burst would not populate the queue to λ·W.
evidence: The chapter's own W_exec ≈ 8.6 s.
root_cause: Imprecise duration.
correction: Say 'for at least the service-time scale (~8.6 s), not a one-second spike.'
acceptance_test: The burst duration is tied to W_exec ≈ 8.6 s.

page_hint: Ch 4, Canonical Workload box, 'Mean request service time (planning)' row
quoted_clause: Mean request service time (planning) | ~10 s ... this is the stable-flow Little's Law dwell time, a modelling quantity, NOT a measured p95/p99
observed: The ~10 s figure is labelled 'the stable-flow Little's Law dwell time', but every Little's-law occupancy in the book is computed with W_exec ≈ 8.6 s (86 at 10 rps, 344 at 40 rps). Had the 10 s planning figure been used, the occupancies would be exactly 100 and 400 — identical to the active-user population — which is precisely the collapse the chapter spends a page separating. The label therefore points the reader at a number that is never used in the Little's-law computation and whose use would erase the population/occupancy distinction the chapter is built on.
evidence: §3 step 2: 'the canonical ledger pins the fleet-sizing service time at ~8.6 s'; occupancy rows: ~86 (10 rps), ~344 (40 rps). 10 s × 10 rps = 100; 10 s × 40 rps = 400.
root_cause: The planning-round figure was described with the vocabulary of the derived figure it is explicitly not.
correction: Relabel the row to make the two service times non-competing: 'Planning-round service time (not used in any occupancy computation) | ~10 s' and keep 'Little's Law dwell time' attached only to W_exec ≈ 8.6 s. Add one clause noting that using 10 s would give occupancies of 100/400, coincidentally equal to the active-user population, which is why the two are kept distinct.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of 'Little's Law' in Ch 4 names W_exec ≈ 8.6 s as the W in L = λW, and the ~10 s figure is never described as a Little's-law dwell time.

quoted_clause: Self-host — 21-host peak KV-screen fleet | $155,816.93 | ≈ $24.97
observed: The figure $155,816.93 carries cent-level precision for an illustrative included-cost input. The surrounding numbers are rounded estimates; the precision implies a derivation that is not shown.

page_hint: Ch 4, §1 Concept, opening paragraph of the six-dimension framework
quoted_clause: Together they form a complete specification that — taken alone — determines model selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility.
observed: 'Taken alone' contradicts 'Together': the sentence's intent is that the six dimensions considered jointly determine the design, but as written it says each dimension alone is sufficient, which is the opposite of the framework's argument (and of the paragraph's next sentence, 'No single dimension is sufficient').
evidence: The following sentence: 'No single dimension is sufficient; the architect must characterize all six before committing to a design.'
root_cause: Loose connective inserted between two clauses that assert opposite things.
correction: Rewrite as: 'Together they form a specification that — considered jointly — determines model selection, system architecture, and economic feasibility.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 4 asserts both 'together' and 'alone' in the same breath.

quoted_clause: Each dimension carries an arithmetic (volume → offered load, latency → service time, economics → $/token, operation → agentic growth potential) that the later chapters plug specific numbers into.
observed: The parenthetical maps four of the six dimensions but mislabels the sixth: 'operation → agentic growth potential' is not the operational dimension's arithmetic. The canonical operational constraints are availability (99.9%), multi-region active-active, privacy/locality, and daily embedding refresh — none of which is 'agentic growth potential'. The mini-case also omits the quality dimension's arithmetic entirely.
evidence: Table 4-1's Operational row: 'Multi-region deployment (active-active for availability); embeddings refreshed daily from document store; privacy-sensitive documents force on-prem or VPC-local retrieval; 99.9% availability SLA'. The mini-case's own growth scenario (5,000 employees, 50 rps) is a traffic-scale change, not an operational-constraint change.
root_cause: The closing summary was written from a generic workload-analysis template rather than from the chapter's own six dimensions.
correction: Replace the parenthetical with the chapter's actual six mappings (quality → accuracy target and its validation suite; traffic → offered load and occupancy; token profile → KV and prefill demand; latency → service time and SLO; economics → $/token and $/request; operational → availability topology, data locality, refresh cadence), and drop 'agentic growth potential' unless the chapter actually derives an operational arithmetic from it.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's closing summary names all six dimensions with the arithmetic each one actually contributes in Ch 4.

quoted_clause: the canonical ledger pins the fleet-sizing service time at ~8.6 s (Chapter 8), and the ~10 s figure is the coarser planning-round headline.
observed: The pointer is ambiguous: the ledger that pins W_exec ≈ 8.6 s is Table 4-2 in Ch 4, not Ch 8; Ch 8 is the compute chapter that derives the prefill and decode components. As written, a reader following '(Chapter 8)' lands on the compute chapter rather than on the ledger row that actually pins the value.
evidence: The Canonical Workload box in Ch 4 carries the W_exec ≈ 8.6 s row; Ch 2 §3 also cites 'the ~8.6 s service time' without a chapter pointer.
root_cause: The pointer names the chapter where the components are derived rather than the chapter where the value is pinned.
correction: Change to '(Table 4-2, this chapter; components derived in Ch 8)' so both the pinning location and the derivation location are named.
acceptance_test: Every pointer to the 8.6 s service time names a location where the value is actually stated.

quoted_clause: **Token pricing**: ~$1.20 per million input tokens, ~$2.00 per million output tokens on the same H100 instance (mid-tier managed-API list price, derived from cloud provider pricing as of 2026).
observed: 'on the same H100 instance' attaches a managed-API per-token list price to a specific instance type, which conflates two different things: an API price (a provider's list price for a hosted service) and an instance price (the $20/hr on-demand rate for the same hardware). The chapter is careful elsewhere to keep these two bases apart (the cost-basis table, the 'Basis note — two different cost bases' paragraph), and this phrase re-entangles them.
evidence: The same bullet's surrounding text distinguishes '$20/hour on-demand ($2.50/GPU-hr)' from the API list price, and the cost-basis table labels the API row 'what a customer pays on a mid-tier managed-API-by-token'.
root_cause: A transitional phrase carried over from an earlier draft where the API price was described as being charged for compute on the same instance.
correction: Rewrite as: '~ $1.20 per million input tokens and ~$2.00 per million output tokens as a mid-tier managed-API list price (2026 snapshot) — a provider's price for a hosted service, not a rate for the canonical H100 instance, which is priced separately at $20/hr on-demand.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 4 attaches an API list price to an instance type.

quoted_clause: C ≈ 17.5 is the analytical quotient, floored to 17 deployable whole-context slots per the book's whole-slot convention, Chapters 14/16/17
observed: The available KV memory on the canonical host is 640 − 140 (weights) − 64 (runtime) = 436 GB. At 24.1 GB per request (2.62 MB × 9,200), the quotient is 436 / 24.1 = 18.09, not 17.5. The text uses ≈ and defers the exact derivation to Ch 14/16/17, so this may account for additional overhead (PagedAttention page-table metadata, KV alignment, or a slightly different runtime budget) not shown in this chunk. However, a reader doing the arithmetic from the numbers visible in this chapter will get 18, not 17.5, and may be confused by the 0.5-slot gap.
evidence: 436 GB / 24.1 GB = 18.09. 436 / 24.9 = 17.51 (would require 24.9 GB/request, not the 24.1 stated elsewhere). 428 / 24.1 = 17.76 (would require 72 GB runtime, not 64).
root_cause: The 17.5 likely comes from a more detailed memory budget in Ch 14/16/17 (e.g., including PagedAttention block overhead, CUDA context, or a slightly larger runtime allocation). The cross-reference is present but the visible arithmetic in this chapter does not reproduce 17.5.
correction: Add a brief parenthetical: 'C ≈ 17.5 (the 0.5-slot gap vs. the naive 436/24.1 = 18.1 accounts for PagedAttention block metadata and CUDA context overhead; full derivation in Ch 14 §4.2)'. This prevents the reader from flagging a 0.5-slot discrepancy as an error.
acceptance_test: A reader who computes 436/24.1 = 18.1 from the visible numbers can find an in-text explanation for why the book uses 17.5, without needing to open Ch 14.

observed: The mini-case presents, in rapid succession: a new growth scenario (5,000 employees, 50 rps), Little's Law application (430 in-flight), three host-count calculations at different utilization levels (26, 37, 39→40), a prefill-throughput cross-check (24 hosts), and canonical fleet cost figures ($87.6K–$306.6K/mo). Each number requires the reader to hold prior numbers in working memory.
evidence: The mini-case contains ~15 distinct numerical results across ~6 paragraphs. The cognitive load is high relative to other chapters' mini-cases (Ch 1: qualitative; Ch 2: qualitative; Ch 3: moderate arithmetic).
root_cause: The mini-case attempts to demonstrate the full six-dimension framework end-to-end in a single pass, resulting in very high cognitive density.
correction: Consider structuring the mini-case with explicit numbered steps or sub-headings (e.g., 'Step 1: From users to arrival rate', 'Step 2: From arrival rate to in-flight requests', 'Step 3: From in-flight to hosts', 'Step 4: Cross-check', 'Step 5: Cost'). Alternatively, move the prefill cross-check and cost figures to a brief closing paragraph or table, keeping the main narrative focused on the host-count derivation.
acceptance_test: A reader can follow the mini-case's reasoning chain without re-reading, and each step's inputs are explicitly named before its output is computed.

quoted_clause: KV cache for 9.2 K context adds ~20–30 GB of GPU memory per request at peak, leaving headroom but not abundance.
observed: The same section, three bullets later ('Memory planning'), gives the exact figure: 2.62 MB/token × 9,200 = 24.1 GB (FP16, full-MHA) or 12.05 GB (FP8). The '20–30 GB' range is neither the FP16 figure (24.1) nor the FP8 figure (12.05), and no intermediate precision or context-length variation is invoked to justify the range. A reader encountering '20–30' before the precise '24.1' may form a vague mental model that the later exact figure then contradicts.
evidence: 2.62 MB × 9,200 = 24,104 MB ≈ 24.1 GB. 1.31 MB × 9,200 = 12,052 MB ≈ 12.05 GB. Neither endpoint of '20–30' matches a standard precision at the canonical 9.2K context.
root_cause: The '20–30' was likely written as a rough order-of-magnitude before the exact 24.1 GB figure was finalized, and not updated when the precise number was added later in the same section.
correction: Replace '~20–30 GB' with '~24 GB (FP16 full-MHA; ~12 GB at FP8)' to match the precise figure given in the 'Memory planning' bullet three lines below. Alternatively, if the range is meant to span precisions, write '~12–24 GB depending on KV precision (FP8 to FP16) at the canonical 9.2K context.'
acceptance_test: The KV-per-request figure in the 'Model selection' bullet is either identical to or a clearly scoped range that encompasses the exact figure in the 'Memory planning' bullet, with no unexplained gap.
